extraction.name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
extraction.description: A large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox, consisting of 8 languages including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages
extraction.creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert, Facebook AI Research
extraction.inLanguage: en, de, nl, es, fr, pt, it, pl
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Audio files downloaded from LibriVox were downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz and segmented into 10-20 second segments using trained acoustic models with Time-Depth Separable Convolutions and Auto-Segmentation Criterion. Text sources were downloaded from multiple domains including gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org and hathitrust.org using automated parsers and manual approaches.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Read audiobooks from LibriVox based on Project Gutenberg text data
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: Numbers in the text present a unique challenge in the preparation of the dataset. While a library like num2words can be used to convert numbers to words and supports multiple languages, we found that using such tools won't solve the problem in a generic way. For example, a number '401' could be spelled as 'four hundred and one' or 'four-o-one' depending on the context and it is very hard to come up with automated rules to pick one over the other. Further, some of the numbers present in the text could be page numbers and are not read by the speaker. To solve the issue, we align the matched text from the book with the pseudo label and replace the numbers in the matched text with the corresponding aligned words from the pseudo label. While this solution is not perfect as the pseudo label may be not be always have the correct transcription of the audio, we found this to be a reasonably good solution to solve the issue.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Numbers in text were replaced with aligned words from pseudo labels. Heuristics were applied to deal with hyphens and apostrophes, including removing end-of-line hyphenation and replacing rare words with hyphens or apostrophes based on alignment with pseudo labels.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz, segmented into 10-20 second segments based on silence intervals. Text underwent NFKC normalization, removal of unwanted characters (punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols), removal of end-of-line hyphens, and filtering of characters outside valid unicode ranges based on language orthography. Books with corrupted metadata, multiple speakers, or invalid links were removed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Pseudo labels were generated using beam-search decoding with 4-gram language models on trained acoustic models. Transcripts were retrieved by matching pseudo labels to book text using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams and Smith-Waterman alignment. Candidate transcripts with WER >40% compared to pseudo labels were filtered out. Human transcribers corrected development and test set transcripts by listening to audio and correcting clear and obvious errors only.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: WER between generated transcripts and human rated transcripts was measured for development and test sets across all languages, ranging from 1.93% to 12.64% on dev sets and 3.07% to 12.07% on test sets
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Time-Depth Separable (TDS) Convolutions with Auto-Segmentation Criterion (ASG) loss for acoustic modeling, wav2letter@anywhere framework for streaming inference, 4-gram language models for beam-search decoding, TF-IDF for document similarity, Smith-Waterman alignment algorithm, SVM with RBF kernel for gender classification
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender information of speakers was collected and labeled using a gender classifier. Speaker demographics are balanced by gender in development and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset will open new avenues in ASR and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research and promote open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and multilingual ASR
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is read-speech only, derived from audiobooks. Training data is lower than initially available due to unavailable text sources, filtering during transcript retrieval, and filtering during train/valid/test split creation. For some languages, diversity of text source domains made automatic extraction challenging. Some audiobook links were invalid or redirected to incorrect pages.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-To-Speech (TTS) research. Limited supervision datasets (10 hour, 1 hour, and six 10-minute sets) provided for low resource training benchmarks.
